speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity to put our views with regard to this legislation on the record. We do not really want to hold up the Bill or to debate it so long as to prevent its passage. However, there are a number of things which need to be said about the legislation.
First, I should like to deal in a very brief manner with the purpose of this piece of legislation. It asks for certain authorities for the Department of Public Works to undertake various kinds of actions with regard to land and property. It deals with the whole question of lease-purchase. Apparently the Government has been carrying on these practices for a number of years. Now its authority to undertake these practices is under question because of a ruling from the Chair with regard to the use of votes in the House. The legislation asks for the Minister of Public Works and the Department of Public Works to have various authorities to carry on real estate development in a manner in which they have already done.
We have no serious objection to the Government having this authority. In fact, in his report the Auditor General recommended that the authority of the Department be clarified. Our

December 17, 1984
Public Works Act
real concern is not so much with the exact wording of the legislation or the exact legislative authority of the Department. More specifically, it is with how the Government exercises its authority.
I should like to put on the record our concerns about how the Government has exercised the authority which Parliament has given it. We cannot allow this to pass without comment. I want to draw the attention of the Committee to the Auditor General's report because two of its chapters were devoted to the Department of Public Works.
The Auditor General is an officer of the Elouse. He has been given the responsibility of ensuring that we have adequate information to make financial decisions in the Chamber. Obviously the making of financial decisions is the purpose of the Chamber itself. The Auditor General draws our attention to public works and says that the federal Government has been doing a horrendous job in looking after its real estate and the millions of dollars which it spends on property leases. The Auditor General simply condemns the way in which the Government has been handling its real estate. He says that it does not manage its $40 billion to $60 billion worth of property in a manner that in any way recognizes the value of that property, that the Government often overpays for property and that it often takes space which it does not need. Those are three very serious indictments of the Government's practice with regard to real estate management. It does not recognize the value of the property, often overpays for property and takes space that it does not need.
[DOT] (mo)
While the Department of Public Works need adequate legislative authority to carry on the business of providing accommodation for government purposes, it is crucial that this be done in a way that recognizes the concerns of ordinary Canadian citizens about economy and government and the fact that we must get fair value for our taxes. If this kind of practice were allowed to continue indefinitely, this House would have to cease to give authority to the Department of Public Works to do that which is necessary in order for government to carry on its day-to-day business, namely providing accommodation for government departments which provide services to Canadians.
We are dealing with a very serious matter. It has to do fundamentally with how the Government handles the taxpayers' dollar. The Auditor General's report contains two full chapters of numerous case studies outlining the way the Department of Public Works handles real estate. The Auditor General describes that as shameful. It would make a private property manager blush with shame.
I am outlining these concerns which the Auditor General has brought to our attention in the hope that the Government will respond to them. While we give them the legislative authority they need to carry on the day-to-day work of the Government, they must answer to us for the way that they use or abuse this authority. I hope they will do that today. I must say that those practices outlined by the Auditor General were
carried out under a previous Government; therefore, this Government cannot be indicted for those practices. However, if these practices continue or if the Government does not take corrective measures, measures that can be seen to be effective, there will be good reason to indict this Government's handling of real estate.
The Auditor General said that the Department of Public Works often failed to follow Treasury Board guidelines and, in fact, government departments failed to follow directives of the Department of Public Works. This has come about because there is no effective mechanism in place whereby the Department can ensure compliance with its directives. This is one area in which the Department has a responsibility, and the Government and the Minister have the responsibility, to assure this House that this is being changed. In other words, an effective mechanism must be put in place to ensure that the directives of Treasury Board and of the Department are followed.
S)
I must say in passing that it surprises me that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) could not find the time to be present in the House today. Perhaps later on his colleague will share with us why the Minister is not here at a time when legislation involving his Department is before the House.
The Auditor General was so concerned about the handling of real state that when he was asked by the press whether or not he would recommend the firing of the Deputy Minister of Public Works, obviously a serious matter, he responded by saying that it was not his job to tell the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) how to manage public affairs but that if a real estate manager in the private sector were to handle property in the way the Government's managers have handled it, he or she would be given the pink slip. We are facing a serious question here, Mr. Chairman. How does one hold civil servants accountable for the property for which they are given responsibility by this Parliament?
Obviously the previous Minister who was responsible for this property when it was so mismanaged is no longer in office. In effect, he has been held accountable by the people. The people have relieved him of his responsibilities. However, what happens when the properties for which a senior civil servant is responsible are mismanaged in a blatant way? Does the Government have the responsibility to judge and to say that the management of that property is incompetent and the person who has been managing the property should be removed from his or her duties? Does the Government then bring in someone who can handle that property responsibly? If the Government does not share that view, does it have an alternative view that would assure us that property will not continue to be mismanaged but will be handled in a responsible way in the future? These are serious matters which I hope the Government will address in debate today.
The Auditor General has brought to our attention a number of cases involving the management of these real estate problems. For example, the Department of Public Works rented a
December 17, 1984

54,000 square metre building in 1982 at a cost of $154 million over a 10-year period without getting Treasury Board approval. Can you imagine making an expenditure of $154 million over a 10-year period, Mr. Chairman, without receiving Treasury Board approval?

Certainly it was the Liberals but the Liberals are no longer in office. The Conservatives are in office and we need to hear from the new Government about its specific, credible plans to assure us that this will never happen again. What will the Government do to assure us that $154 million will never again be spent by the Department of Public Works without Treasury Board approval? Will a procedure be put in place to correct that?
The Auditor General also found some $63,122,000 in excess payments involving some 12 leases. The Auditor General has been documenting the overpayments made by the Department of Public Works. Now, $63 million is a lot of money, Mr. Chairman. At this time of very high unemployment, that kind of money could be used to supplement the Canada Works Program, for example, which at this time is in bad need of additional appropriations. I would like to know from the Government how it will assure us that there will be no more excess payments. What new procedures will be put in place to assure us that the Government will pay fair value for property that it leases but that it will not overpay? We should have a response from the Government on that matter.
The Auditor General recommended that the Government take a close look at lease-purchase agreements. That is central to the legislation which is before the House today. The legislation clarifies and confirms the authority which the Department has in entering into lease-purchase arrangements. By the lease-purchase agreements, the Government agrees to rent a building for a period of time, and at the end of the rental period the Government purchases the building for a fixed amount. As a consequence, very large sums of money are tied up. It is not a trivial matter; in fact, the Auditor General has identified $1,919,600,000. Almost $2 billion is tied up in lease-purchase arrangements. It is a very heavy responsibility for the Government. The Government must examine how it handles lease-purchase arrangements.
The Auditor General has indicated that these agreements may cost the Crown more than if the Government borrowed the money and built the buildings. In other words, lease-purchase arrangements may cost the public purse more than if the Government built the buildings. For example, the Auditor General studied four lease-purchase agreements which totalled $762.9 million. The Auditor General found that if the Govern-
Public Works Act
ment had borrowed money and built the buildings at the same price as the developer, the cost would have been $85.8 million less over 35 years. In other words, it would have cost the taxpayers $85.8 million less if the Government had built the buildings rather than going the route of the lease-purchase arrangement.
It is incumbent upon the new Minister of Public Works and his Department to assure us that further consideration will be given to the whole question of lease-purchase agreements, as well as to assure us that lease-purchase arrangements will be handled in such a way that they will not cost taxpayers additional money. Why should we lease-purchase if it is better for the Government to borrow the money and build the buildings? That question must be examined.
The Auditor General also raised a question about the way the Government handles real estate and the way it utilizes that space. Is the space needed? Is it used? In using the figures of the Government, the Auditor General found that over the past five years the Government has had about 700,000 square metres of unoccupied space, at a cost of approximately $25 million per year. In these times when the public dollar is scarce-as the Government itself has said-it is important that the Government tell us now what policies and procedures it is going to put in place which will assure us that existing government space will be used and that it will not acquire space which will simply sit empty. What kind of system will the Government put in place to assure us of that?
There is one other area covered by the Auditor General's report which I feel is crucial and should be dealt with today by the Government. The Auditor General found that the federal Department of Public Works withheld information from the federal Cabinet when it leased three downtown Ottawa office buildings two years ago from Campeau Corporation for a total of $400 million. Because this essential information was not provided to Cabinet, it gave up an opportunity to obtain a building worth $46.5 million for $15 million. It is bad enough, Mr. Chairman, when Governments do not share information with Parliament, but when civil servants fail to provide information to Cabinet, the system becomes totally unworkable. So 1 would like to hear some assurances that the Government is going to make sure it receives all information before it makes decisions with regard to public works.
To sum up briefly, Mr. Chairman, the authority which is being asked for today appears to us to be legitimate. The problem has been the abuse of that authority in the past. We would like to know how this Government is going to assure Parliament that this abuse will stop and that the public dollar will be used wisely and with due prudence. I would like to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary-and I wonder why the Minister is not here-as to just what procedures are going to be put in place in order to make sure that the taxpayers' money is not wasted. I would like to know specifically how the Government is going to hold its civil servants accountable in order to ensure that the job which needs to be done is done.

Mir. Stewart: First of all, Mr. Chairman, let me say that I was going to speak on the Bill previously. However, when it was referred to Committee of the Whole I did not feel there was any need to waste the time of the House as we pretty well have agreement.

With respect to lease-purchases, I will say that, of course, the Auditor General has made his views well known and I do not disagree with him. However, we must acknowledge that where Crown finance is not possible or preferable, lease-purchasing does clearly result in cost saving or cost avoidance to the Government, and ultimately to the taxpayers of this country. I have with me, Mr. Chairman, lease-purchase agreements for the Esplanade Laurier and C. D. Howe buildings which total some $24,668,890. The total rent in 1983-84 for comparable space in Ottawa would have amounted to $45,119,760. In this case the Government has an actual saving of $20,450,870.
These purchases are not always wrong. There are some advantages, of course, in the fact that there is fixed rental for 35 years and it will only vary up or down every five years. The operating and management fees are also fixed. The Crown will eventually own the building and has control over the quality of the building, ensuring that the performance specifications are met.
For the information of the Hon. Member, Mr. Chairman, an analysis is made in each case to compare lease-purchase to leasing and Crown financed construction. These analyses are given to Treasury Board. Let me assure the Hon. Member that the Minister will work very closely with Treasury Board in order to make sure the effective changes the Hon. Member is so concerned about-as we all are-will be put in place and that things which were not done properly in the past will be done in the future to everyone's satisfaction. I believe I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that all lease-purchase projects will be done in the most effective manner through Treasury Board and the Minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1955 Canada has conducted mid-decade censuses. The censuses provide important data to all sectors of government and business. This information is used to assess population movements which affect transfer payments, to assess labour market trends, income distribution, living conditions, and many other things.
The information from censuses helps businesses make marketing decisions. The officials of the Minister of Supply and Services admitted that various organizations have protested the cancellation of the 1986 census, but they would not name the associations. One of those joining the list of those protesting the cancellation of the 1986 census is the Canadian Home Builders Association. The Association has 5,000 members, and
their objections to the cancellation of the 1986 census are representative of the protests of many others.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the report of the chief actuary of the Department of Insurance tabled in the House of Commons this year attention is focused on the serious underfunding of the Canada Pension Plan. If contribution rates are not increased, costs of benefits and expenses will exceed contributions next year. The CPP account would grow until 1994 and then would start to decline. The account would be exhausted by the year 2004, which is just 20 years hence.
Benefit levels and contribution rates cannot be altered under existing legislation without provincial agreement. Therefore I would urge both the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and his provincial counterparts to take urgent action to preserve the integrity of the Canada Pension Plan. If changes are not made now, there will be no funds left in 20 years with which to pay pensions to those Canadians who are now, by law, obliged to contribute hard-earned cash into the scheme.

subtopic: INSECTICIDE POISONING-EFFECTS ON FARMERS
INSECTICIDE POISONING-EFFECTS ON FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the events at Bhopal have focused world attention on the agony of death from pesticide poisoning as more than 2,000 people died horrible deaths. 1 want to raise the consciousness of the House to the everyday pesticide poisonings that occur amongst the world's farmers. Six thousand farmers, more than three times as many as died at Bhopal, are killed by pesticides every year.
In addition, more than 500,000 farmers are poisoned by pesticides each year. Some recover; some are harmed permanently. These poisonings occur in the developed countries as well, but the majority occur in the underdeveloped countries. The chemical industry says that the reason is illiteracy, but it is also due to a reduction in legislative requirements restricting usage in those countries. Chemicals not permitted here because testing has shown them to be unsafe to the users are used in less developed countries.
In addition to reduced regulation, newly industrialized countries like Mexico, Brazil, and India have tough import taxes to stimulate the growth of domestic chemical industries. They are, to use a familiar phrase, open for business. I urge the House to take action on the clear need for adequate testing, and the inception of a policy to monitor the cumulative effects upon humans who must handle farm pesticides in the fields in our country so that eventually we will know the effects on users and avoid this continued needless waste of farmers' lives.

subtopic: CALL FOR RESTORATION
CALL FOR RESTORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most races from the most ancient times to the present have prohibited murder and severely punished offenders.
First degree murder by definition means "the unlawful killing of one or more human beings, by another or others with malice aforethought".
One can easily realize that in this age of violent weaponry, murder is made all too easy.
One cannot exist in a society where one's self or one's family and friends are at the mercy of those who go about casually taking lives.
The stupid, the evil, and yes, some who are insane, seek to solve their real or imagined problems with murder. And they have also been known to commit murder for no reason at all.
Murder, Mr. Speaker, bears the highest priority for any nation in social prevention and retaliation.
There are crimes committed against others which cannot be waived or forgotten. Murder is such a crime.
Therefore it is my hope that the people of Canada will soon be given the satisfaction for which they have been clamoring since capital punishment was abolished in 1976, the satisfaction of a free vote, and 1 emphasize a free vote, which was not certainly the case in 1976, on capital punishment, the outcome of which, I believe, would satisfy the majority of the people of Canada.

December 17, 1984
Investment Canada Act INVESTMENT CANADA ACT

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, December 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-15 is to replace the Foreign Investment Review Act and the review process it enables the Government to carry out with a new Act creating Investment Canada. The Government says its purpose is to attract foreign investment to Canada and, as a result, create jobs and other benefits for our economy.
The kindest thing I can say about the Bill is that while it may be well-intention, it is thoroughly misguided. In my view, it will not bring the results intended. It will do just the reverse. If the Bill passes, it will seriously weaken the ability of the Government to ensure that the limited kinds of foreign investment covered by the present Foreign Investment Review Act brings real and significant benefits to Canadians, especially when it comes to jobs, but also including such factors as more research and development, more sourcing of parts and components here, and more exports.
Even though the level of foreign control in some sectors here has declined somewhat in recent years, Canada still has more of its economy owned and controlled outside of its borders than any other developed country. Study after study has shown that foreign investment, while it can bring benefits to our economy, has real costs attached to it for Canadians. Yes, it may bring access to markets and new technology and jobs that might not otherwise be here, but the evidence is clear that foreign-controlled firms generally do less research and development in our country. They purchase more of their parts and components outside of Canada and they tend to export less than their Canadian-controlled counterparts.
A recent Statistics Canada report indicates that foreign-controlled firms tend to import substantially more of the parts required for their products than Canadian-controlled firms. The Progressive Conservative Party's task force on Canada's high-tech future issued a report earlier this year. It stated that recent data indicates that research and development intensity of foreign subsidiaries tends to lag behind domestically owned operations of comparable magnitude. All this means a branch plant economy for Canada, one that will not be able to prosper, much less survive effectively in a tough world marketplace which demands of countries and their companies a high degree of efficiency, productivity and innovation.
Foreign direct investment which owns or controls companies and assets in Canada means key decisions about our economic well-being are made outside our borders. It means outflows of interest and dividends to the extent where they help to create and perpetuate balance of payment problems. I have to say that as long as our capital needs cannot be filled from domestic sources, there is certainly a place for foreign capital in Canada, a welcome place to the extent that it brings real
benefits to our economy, to the extent that these benefits can be maximized and their cost minimized.
That is the purpose of the FIRA process. It is not primarily to block foreign direct investment, but to strive to maximize its benefits and to minimize its costs for Canadians, in short, to ensure a good deal for the foreign investors and for Canadians. That it has been able to do this is demonstrated by the high level of approvals, averaging 92 per cent since the process began in 1974. Until recently, at least, this high percentage of approvals was criticized by many as showing that the FIRA process was too lax. In reality, it shows that investors have been able to meet the test of the significant benefit to Canada in such things as more jobs, research and development and exports, either in their original applications or as a result of negotiations by the Government, resulting in a good deal for the investors and for Canada.
This high level of approval helps demonstrate that FIRA has not discouraged or prevented from entering Canada foreign direct investment needed by and beneficial to Canada. This fact is also demonstrated by statistics on foreign capital movements, showing that these inflows in the years after FIRA began operating in 1974 were substantially higher than in the years preceding its beginnings. In fact, foreign direct investment in Canada has steadily increased each year since the FIRA process began in 1974, perhaps dropping somewhat only in the depths of the recession which affected not only Canada, but the entire world. During that recession, capital flows slowed down everywhere, including the United States. However, in the first quarter of 1984, foreign direct investment in Canada reached its highest level in many years.
All of this demonstrates one important point. Capital moves to a country in response to expectation of profits. It comes when investors seek the opportunity to make a profit. Dismantling FIRA, replacing it with a truncated remnant called Investment Canada, will do nothing to respond to this essential point. The Bill does nothing to create more real opportunities for profit by investors.
In any event, FIRA never dealt with more than about 3 per cent of foreign direct investment. It does not deal at all with the largest potential source of foreign investment, the existing foreign-controlled sector in Canada. Projects for expansion, modernization or for new plants by firms already here do not require review and approval by the Government. Investment in the form of loans does not require approval by the Government under FIRA, nor does equity investment in quantities not sufficient to control an enterprise.
To repeat, the Investment Canada Bill does nothing to help our economy offer more prospects to make a profit, more prospects of success to potential investors, whether foreign or Canadian. Nor does it create markets for their production, another factor bringing investment to a country. It does nothing to create consumer or industry demand in Canada or abroad. Using this Bill to dismantle FIRA will not bring more beneficial investment from abroad, either in the limited area covered by the Foreign Investment Review Act-and basically this covers takeovers of companies and new projects by compa-
December 17, 1984

nies not already established here-or the much larger area of the kinds of investment not dealt with by the present FIRA process.
A very serious flaw among the many in the Bill is that while the Government says the new Investment Canada agency will have a mandate to encourage Canadian investment as well as foreign, there is nothing in the Bill offering any real encouragement or incentive to Canadian investment. Yet there is a great potential for more investment by Canadians in their own economy. Canadians have a very high rate of savings; at least twice that of people in the United States. The basic thrust of the Government is to seek out foreign investors to sell off more of our economy abroad rather than to give priority to encouraging our capital needs to be filled from Canadian sources. However, a substantial capacity to do so definitely exists in our country according to studies done by the Investment Dealers' Association.
In September 1981, the President of the Investment Dealers' Association said in part:
Our capacity to generate savings in Canada is now very large and growing quickly. It would appear that some 94 per cent... of the new savings required in the 1980s can be generated in Canada . . . the balance of 6 per cent will have to be imported.
He went on to say:
This reliance on foreign capital will be slightly less than over the past 10 years and indeed on a net basis will disappear entirely mid-way through the 1990s.
Last week, my office asked the staff of the President of the Investment Dealers' Association of Canada if it could update those projections. We were told that they are generally the same except that they would now indicate that 95 per cent rather than 94 per cent of the savings needed for the investment required by our country in the 1980s can be generated right here in Canada.
The Minister has said that Investment Canada will be given the job of going out and encouraging investment in Canada. However, that has always been the job of the entire Department of what is now called Regional Industrial Expansion and its regional offices across Canada, the Department of External Trade, especially its overseas trade commissioner services, as well as other high-tech Departments like Communications. Apparently the Tories intend to change all that and limit the work of the Government in encouraging investment to the tiny agency they intend to call Investment Canada. It will be composed of no more than the present staff of FIRA, some 130 people, many of whom will have to carry out the remnants of the review process that will still exist if this Bill is passed. I submit that the results will be less effort and less real work by the Government to promote beneficial investment for Canada than was the case under the previous Liberal Government.
The decision made by American Motors after it had been taken over by Renault to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in expanding its Brampton, Ontario, plant and to increase jobs there substantially came after negotiations by the previous Liberal Government through its Department of Regional
Investment Canada Act
Industrial Expansion and FIRA. The decision of MBB of Germany to create a joint venture with Fleet Aircraft, a Canadian company, to manufacture helicopters in Fort Erie also came following negotiations by the previous federal Government through Regional Industrial Expansion and the FIRA process. As well, this was generally the case with the deal with Bell Helicopter to establish a plant near Montreal. This also involved investments of hundreds of millions of dollars. These are concrete examples to show how the previous Liberal Government helped attract beneficial foreign investment to Canada involving new technologies, world competitive products and thousands of jobs.
The FIRA process, rather than discouraging or preventing this kind of investment, helped maximize the benefits flowing from it to Canadians, and the investors in question certainly were not discouraged or turned away by the FIRA process. The present Conservative Government, through recently cutting back and limiting of the Industrial and Regional Development Program of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and now apparently intending to concentrate the Government's investment promotion efforts in little Investment Canada, will be decreasing the likelihood of getting more of these kinds of good deals for Canada and for Canadian workers.
Also, if this Bill passes, the Government will no longer be able to review any new investment projects proposed by a company not yet established here or by one established here if the proposal is totally unrelated to what that company is already doing, regardless of the size of the project. This means the Government will not be able to negotiate to seek binding commitments from the investor to maximize the benefits to Canada in areas of jobs, research and development and world product mandates as a condition of allowing the transaction to proceed. In other words, the bargaining power which helped the Government to confirm that there were realistically defined maximum benefits for Canadian workers and the Canadian economy in projects like AMC in Brampton and MBB-Fleet in Fort Erie or Bell Helicopter near Montreal will no longer be there.
As well, if this Bill passes, no direct takeover of a firm in Canada worth less than $5 million and no indirect takeover where control of the parent changes abroad worth less than $50 million will be subject to review by the Government. The door will be open for firms below these thresholds to be taken over and closed down and the products they make exported into Canada by the new parent firms from abroad with jobs being lost to Canada.
If the Bill passes, in addition to the risk of this very difficult kind of situation, the door is open for firms below these thresholds to be taken over and, if not closed down, then turned largely into warehousing operations with the production and technology they have developed transferred abroad. The Government will not be able to do anything to protect Canadian jobs and Canadian technology. As well, the Government will not be able to negotiate and get commitments not simply

December 17, 1984
Investment Canada Act
to preserve but also to confirm additional jobs and other economic benefits if takeovers are below these new thresholds.
The Minister spoke about not wanting to deal with applications to set up peanut stands. If I can mix a metaphor, that is a very big red herring. In many sectors and especially those in the high technology areas, firms are generally small, especially in the beginning stages. As organizations like the Canadian Federation of Independent Business always remind us, Canada's small businesses, generally Canadian-controlled, are a major potential source of new jobs and innovation. The Conservative Government, in pushing for the adoption of Bill C-15, is ready to see all this lost to Canada. Also, many firms below these thresholds may be small but they are major employers and are very big in the economies of the communities in which they are located. This point has also escaped the Conservative sellout artists.
Of course, every government organization and every government program which has been in existence for a number of years has room for updating and improvement. This includes FIRA. As Minister, I made changes in the administrative side of FIRA which did not require legislation to achieve. These changes were made to simplify, smooth out and greatly speed up that process. It is strange that the Conservatives, in developing this Bill, left intact one of the major points of concern both for business and the general public regarding the existing Foreign Investment Review Act. I am talking about the high degree of confidentiality which the law requires of all FIRA operations. Among other things, this confidentiality prevents the Government, except in very general terms in FIRA reports, from setting out the facts on the thousands of additional jobs, research and development and exports which resulted from the application of the FIRA process.
As well, it is strange, in light of the concerns about the so-called arbitrariness of the current FIRA process, which I believe are not justified, that this Bill would make the successor to that process truly arbitrary. It places all powers of decision over the few large takeover cases, which would still be reviewed and could involve the futures of thousands of workers, in the hands of the Minister alone rather than having those decisions be collective decisions of Cabinet.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would say that we do need more investment, both foreign and Canadian but especially Canadian. However, if this Bill is passed, it will not be the way to go about getting it. This Bill, if passed, would weaken the ability of our Government to protect existing Canadian jobs and technology. It will weaken the Government's ability to obtain a realistically defined maximum in terms of more jobs and other economic benefits for Canadians from direct foreign investment.
This Bill should be looked at along with the harm to our cultural identity which will likely be caused by the cuts to the CBC budget, the Prime Minister's speech in New York confirming his desire to have even more of our economy sold off abroad, as well as the Government's seeming willingness to
undermine our political and economic sovereignty and prospects for growth through pushing for complete continental free trade. All this forms a disturbing pattern. It is one that should greatly alarm Canadians. Over-all, the Bill is deeply flawed. It requires a major study by the House as well as by Canadians. It does not deserve the support of the House. Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault):
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-15, An Act respecting investment in Canada, be not now read a
second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak this afternoon to the Bill before the House, an Act respecting investment in Canada. I have been in the field of public economic development policy for five years, and during that time 1 had occasion to examine the work done by the Foreign Investment Review Agency. My conclusion was that dogmatic and ideological considerations have no place in economic development.
Mr. Speaker, representations made by the Opposition, both by the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, have, until now, been highly emotional, ideological and dogmatic. We have seen the damage done by the National Energy Program because it was based mainly on dogmatic considerations. The program was created out of a desire for centralizing control over the oil industry at the federal level, mainly in order to restain the producing provinces which were showing too much independence to the federal, then Liberal, Government's taste.
Mr. Speaker, we have seen the damage done by the 1980 MacEachen budget, which was also based on dogmatic concepts and the desire to weaken the private sector and those people who, according to the Liberal Administration, appeared to favour business methods and development and growth priorities that differred from those sanctioned by the Government at the time. Because Bill C-15 is a step in the right direction towards removing the impact of dogmatism, I am supporting this Bill and I would like to see it referred without delay to the appropriate committee of the House, for thorough analysis in a constructive and a responsible manner, and subsequent amendments as appropriate.
When considering ways of promoting economic development, Mr. Speaker, we should simply ask ourselves whether a given method or measure or the withdrawal of a measure will or will not promote development. That is the question we must ask. Today, environmental protection and employment are some of the aspects that must be considered as a matter of course. We are not talking about development at any cost, on the contrary.
The Bill now before the House recognizes that investment is the linchpin of economic growth and job creation and the key to technological development. That is why we make the assumption that investment in Canada, either by Canadians or non-Canadians, is likely to benefit this country.
The Bill provides for the establishment of a new agency, to be called Investment Canada. It also provides for the review of significant investments by non-Canadians to ensure that the assumption that the investment will benefit Canada is justified. Non-Canadian investors intending to make minor acquisitions or create new businesses need merely notify the agency of their intentions.
This legislation is therefore not sounding the death knell of Canadian ownership or of our pride in our Canadian businesses. It is simply a new Bill that takes a more positive and less dogmatic approach than the legislation it is going to replace.
Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the existing FIRA had approved more than 90 per cent of applications for acquisitions in this
December 17, 1984

country, so the first question that comes to mind is whether the huge amounts budgeted for that exercise have been well spent or even well allocated. Our economy and our country have had other priorities, and I am wondering whether such funds allocated for an exercise which did not seem to be all that essential were indeed wisely allocated, particularly if we consider that, since the advent of FIRA, Canadian ownership has increased regularly despite rising direct foreign investment in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have the CALURA report which contains a table on percentages of foreign controlled non-financial industries in Canada for 1971, 1976 and 1981. As an example, I will refer to a few sectors only. In agriculture, foreign ownership declined by 9 per cent, 32 per cent in mining, 17 per cent in foodstuffs, 28 per cent in primary processing of metals. Overall, foreign ownership in those sectors decreased by 11 per cent, notwithstanding the fact that FIRA approved more than 90 per cent of foreign applications for acquisitions.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to stress that, in the same report, indirect investment is said to have gone up accordingly. That is another aspect of the whole question of foreign investment which I want to discuss. Investments in the form of direct funding are better than investments in the form of debts, because they create jobs and are profitable to the investor and the host country. The investor cannot make profits and declare dividends unless he succeeds.
As stated in a Conference Board of Canada report:
In the 19th century foreign investors favoured this country by buying the bonds of its municipalities and railroads. In the early years of this century such portfolio investment was rapidly superseded by foreign direct investment. The economic significance of this distinction is that direct investment typically involves the transfer form the parent to the affiliate of an intangible and proprietary asset such as technology, managerial control, a unique or differentiated product, or a market position. Alternatively, direct investment may involve backwards integration to ensure security of supply for raw materials used in the parent company's production process. The circumstances surrounding direct investment make it desirable from the investor's point of view for the parent to exercise a managerial control that is not possible with portfolio investment in order to protect its unique and non-transferable assets or market position.

Mr. Speaker, this means that direct investments bring us jobs and profitable businesses. On the other hand, indebtedness creates a return for the foreign creditor while the country in debt has no employment, no productivity or return on its investment. The country with borrowed rather than directly invested capital will find itself with growing debt which affects
Investment Canada Act
inflation and domestic interest rates and undermines its development opportunities.
Indeed, it is because Canada has irresponsibly accumulated debts that we find ourselves in an economic deadend today. Because of that, we found ourselves compelled to agree to policies we find repugnant, such as the 1 per cent increase in sales tax which was advocated by the previous Liberal Government, and the rate increase for various services provided by the Government, and also to impose cut-backs in certain areas. While it is true that most of these cut-backs are related to administrative costs, we hate having to implement them because of the current unemployment problem.
Mr. Speaker, all Hon. Members are aware that an individual can give the appearance of economic stability, affluence and ownership. He can do so by driving a leased car, by living in a house with a 90 per cent mortgage and by buying his clothes with credit cards. However, they also know that, when his income is reduced and he can no longer meet his payments, he is faced with disaster. He may feel that he owns all this, but it is only an illusion of ownership.
Therefore, I believe that as a country under previous governments, we have, in a similar way, increased our indebtedness as opposed to acquiring the kind of direct capital investment that creates jobs and gives us the flexibility required to assume our responsibilities as a just society anxious to look after those who have the direst needs.
Over the last decade, Mr. Speaker, Canada has been driving a rented Buick. It has been entertaining friends at the golf club using a Visa credit card. The most recent bill handed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) added up to at least a $34 billion deficit and an indebtedness of over $150 billion.
It is time we destroy some of those credit cards, Mr. Speaker. Not all of them, of course, because credit is also a tool for economic growth, but some of them.
Moreover, I also believe it is high time we asked ourselves whether we are not entertaining the illusion of ownership, whether our debt is not the one most important amount or property we wholly own.
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that theorists have no place in the area of development. I would like to refer to that study by the Conference Board which commented on the establishment of the screening agency along the lines of the "Gray" report's recommendation.
I am sorry that the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) has left the House, because I think he would be interested in this comment.
The Conference Board stated in its report:

Public and political reaction to the Gray report was in large measure dictated by the foreign investment issue's high public profile and the precarious political balance after the 1972 federal election when I believe the Liberal administration had

December 17, 1984
Investment Canada Act
a minority. The key factor in the situation was the New Democratic Party's espousal of some form of foreign investment screening. Finding itself pressured by the Waffle group, a radical fragment of its Party, the NDP in turn exploited its position as the Party holding the balance of power to exert pressure on the ruling Liberals. In this atmosphere, the Gray report rapidly became a cause celebre.

A celebrated law case. And the report goes on to state that- [English]
There are a number of academics, politicians and business leaders who are sympathetic to the notion of abolishing FIRA. It is difficult, however, to assess whether these forces opposing FIRA are capable of overcoming the political interests which view FIRA as an important electoral and policy symbol. It goes on to say that the suggestion to permit new investments to enter Canada without being subjected to FIRA would certainly alleviate FIRA's caseload and therefore speed up the process. New business applications comprise about one half of the total applications FIRA receives. This suggests that on close scrutiny FIRA's decision on new acquisitions is based on the fact that it does not believe that these bring significant benefit to Canada. In addition, some domestic companies may not welcome the idea of an open door policy regarding new investment since FIRA provides these companies with an element of protection from foreign competitors. I know, Mr. Speaker, that this is an unhealthy sign for a trading nation such as we are, one which needs strong industry and must cease to take refuge behind non-tariff barriers.
As Hon. Members know, there is both fear of growing protectionism in our major commercial trading partners and a growing need to free trade between nations in order to increase employment growth in various countries, including ours. Canada should be working toward strengthening its industrial sectors to meet competition at home and to go out and secure other markets outside. Therefore, we must strike a balance between leaving our weaker sectors exposed to competition and making every effort to seek new markets, which will only be open to us if we are ready to be open to them. Countries which need to sell to us their specialties would not look kindly on our closing our markets to them or their investments. The whole question of world economic stability and debt service in developing countries is also tied to our ability to trade the world over. This is why-

[ Translation]
-because we are not dealing any death blow to the principle of essential screening nor to the protection of Canadian ownership with this legislation, Mr. Speaker. On the contrary, we are introducing a positive investment dimension, combined with a realistic protection of our best Canadian interests.
I note in the Bill, Mr. Speaker, that the responsibilities of the Minister and of the agency are to encourage business investment by such means and in such manner as they deem appropriate, assist Canadian businesses to exploit opportunities for investment and technological investment.
I found out in the Conference Board report I was referring to that France has taken such an open approach. Although France has a Socialist Government, that Government is sufficiently concerned with the country's development to realize it must provide other nations and private enterprise with incentives to come in and invest. Therefore, in their screening provisions, they have that positive aspect we want somehow to copy here, that is to help businesses acknowledge investments here while being very careful to protect Canadian ownership and interests.
Its responsibilities also include making studies of investment both at the national and international level. I noticed that in the definition given of France's screening agency, there was the same attitude, namely to provide an investment information service to promote economic growth, to help develop economic and industrial policies that foster investment and to ensure that investment notification and review is done in accordance with the legislation. I see here some very positive aspects. I see here some serious and responsible interventions on the part of the Minister and his agency in the area of investment in Canada. I do not see what we have been hearing during the last few days, which was that our interests are being sold down the river and that we have forgotten and neglected our pride in Canadian ownership.
Mr. Speaker, I think this Bill is a valid one which should be given serious consideration in committee, with no thought of partisanship, keeping in mind what binds us together which is our country's interests, the interests of today's youth who are unemployed and also the interests of future generations. In considering this legislation, we should make this the first Bill where Parliament has been able to agree that the interests of young Canadians, of the elderly who need funds for their pension plans, of women who need a sound economy to attain equality, are of primary importance. In committee, Mr. Speaker, we ought to consider this Bill carefully and make it one of which we can all be proud, whatever our political affiliation.

1 want to thank my colleague for asking these questions.
In reply to the first one dealing with the limits set to exonerate acquisitions under $5 million, I believe that this should in fact be discussed in committee to determine whether this amount is realistic and will help protect small businesses. According to available data and in view of the fact that the number of acquisitions approved by the former screening agency did not cause any harm to small businesses, the amount of $5 million chosen by the Minister seemed appropriate to solve the problem of how not to interfere with investment favourable to Canada while protecting small businesses which may be weaker than others. However, this is a very serious
Investment Canada Act
subject which should be reviewed in committee, and this is why I would like us to reach this stage as soon as possible instead of spending many hours in the House letting off steam, which I do not consider particularly constructive.
As for the second question of why a change should be made at this point, it is because, as I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, over 90 per cent of the applications submitted were approved by the screening agency, which might suggest that the rules were not realistic. Otherwise, perhaps half of the applications or even more would have been turned down. In fact, nearly all the applications were approved in spite of the fact that they were screened at a cost, I believe, of $6,000 each. This is why a change is needed and it is partly motivated by the wish to reduce expenses and to determine whether existing agencies truly play an essential role, especially when they are costly to run, and whether we could not obtain the same results at a lesser cost. This is one aspect of the matter.
Another aspect has to do with indirect transfers between non-Canadians. If a business was already controlled by foreign interests and everything was going well, we have to ask ourselves this question: Does the state have any business interfering in an exchange between two individuals or moral persons for reasons which are mostly ideological? However, this is another issue that my hon. colleague will certainly want to discuss in committee.
As for the last question asked by the Hon. Member, or rather his comment on the situation in France, I believe that he will agree that France has recently taken a new direction, because earlier, the tendency was mostly to direct the economy in a traditional manner with traditional socialistic methods.
But people realized that France does not exist in a vacuum, that she lives in a world where trade reaches beyond frontiers, otherwise there cannot be economic growth in the country.
Canada is in the same situation, perhaps more so for Canada because we do not have the Common Market which does give some protection to France. I therefore think that France is leaning much more on our side than the Hon. Member would care to admit, but I have the impression that we are headed in the right direction and that other countries, for which it is not a traditional approach, seem to be doing the same thing.
But again those are aspects which will be debated in committee, I hope.

What is the primary reason, as I see it, for the six-month hoist? Why should this Bill not be allowed to proceed unless certain actions are taken by the Government of Canada? Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker. The very Minister who introduced this Bill did so to promote economic development in Canada and to try to create an atmosphere for investment, not only, as the Bill says, for foreign countries through FIRA, but for ordinary Canadians and Canadian investment. But that very Minister had to cut $175 million from the industrial and regional development program in his Department, what he calls adjustments to regulations. This program provides the very industrial incentives that businessmen need when they want to develop in high unemployment areas of Canada. I am talking primarily about a province like Newfoundland. That very Minister, Mr. Speaker, also approved reductions in what he called other Drie industrial incentive programs to the tune of $25 million for a total of $200 million.
Prior to about two years ago we always had the DREE program in the high unemployment areas. That program guaranteed 25 per cent of the capital costs. Along came the departmental reorganization into DRIE. All of a sudden, costs amounted to 50 per cent to 60 per cent overhead plus 65 per cent of the cost of a study. Now we see there is drastic reduction in the very Department of the Minister who brings in a Bill and says, "We want to encourage investment in Canada by foreigners and by Canadians". Then there was the industrial training program with its cuts. In other words you have a businessman wanting to set up in a high unemployment area of Canada. You could always use what was called on-the-job training. Cuts were announced by the Government amounting to $40 million.
First, if you want to set up, you cannot. That has been cut. If you want to train people, you cannot. That has been cut. The Government was not content with that. It looked at modes
December 17, 1984

of transportation from high unemployment areas. The Government said, "Let us take a crack at that". What about transportation by air? An investor says, "I want to move certain commodities by air". The Government then announces that there will be an air cargo tax coming into effect in 1987. What if you want to go by rail, or by land? We have fare increases, and operating costs. He said: Mr. Speaker, for a number of years I have been submitting Private Member's Bills to this House, aimed at correcting certain discrepancies in the Official Languages Act, and I must say it is a source of great satisfaction to me that every time in the past eight or nine years that I presented a Bill, there was a good debate in the House and the Bill was given serious consideration by the Committee on Official Languages. Moreover, suggestions made in these Bills were adopted both by the Committee and the Government.
Today's legislation, Bill C-203, is therefore one more in a series of Private Members' Bills presented by me in the House, and I may remind Hon. Members that the last time the matter was discussed in 1980, the Bill or Bills were referred to the Special Joint Committee on Official Languages for study and consideration, resulting in very substantial amendments both to the Criminal Code and to the Official Languages Act.
To give Hon. Members some historical background, in 1978, Bill C-210 which I presented in the House was aimed at correcting certain discrepancies in the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1970 and deleted certain references to bilingual districts, which, in any case, were never established. Hon. Members will recall that at each census, a committee was to be formed to examine the establishment of bilingual districts.

These bilingual districts were examined by two commissions, after the 1971 and 1981 census, and Parliament never followed up their recommendations. When the Government fails to follow the recommendations made by a committee established under an Act of Parliament, one would think the legislation was not terribly important and that anomalies such as bilingual districts, for instance, should be deleted from our statutes.
The same Bill C-210, in 1978, gave the defendant the right to be heard and judged by a court or a judge speaking the language of the defendant, and the Bill also amended certain Acts including the Railway Act, the Winding-up Act, the Bank Act and a number of other statutes in order to remove certain discrepancies from the Statutes. I would like to give one example which I find rather obvious, and that is the Railway Act.
The Railway Act provides that, in Quebec, the station agent shall write, with white chalk on a blackboard, the arrival and departure of trains as well as the time of overdue trains. The Act states clearly that this is to be done in French and English in Quebec, whereas it is to be done in English in the other provinces. Well, we all know that today that measure does not apply only in Quebec, thanks to the Official Languages Act. I have colleagues from Ontario, western and eastern Canada- and yourself, Mr. Speaker-who would readily acknowledge that nowadays the proper thing to do for a national carrier is to abide by the Official Languages Act and that it is irregular to have in our statute books a provision under which that procedure applies only in Quebec. The same thing applies to banks, the same thing applies to liquidations: only in Quebec must it be done in French and English, which leads one to believe that the rest of Canada is unilingual and anglophone.
In any case, here I am again with Bill C-203, an Act to amend the Official Languages Act, and I move that it be read the second time and referred to the Standing Joint Committee on Official Languages Policy and Programs. Mr. Speaker, Bill C-203 is similar to others like C-214 and C-210 which I introduced in Parliament in May 1980 and whose general intent was to be given approval by the Special Joint Committee on Official Languages. Indeed, in its fourth and fifth reports, the committee refers to the recommendations contained in Bill C-214.
Bill C-203 is based primarily on considerations of a legal nature, but also on considerations of a political nature, in the non-partisan sense of the word. If I may sum up those two aspects in a single statement, I would say that this Parliament must consolidate one of the main foundations of our federal system, the principle of linguistic equality, by deleting from our statutes any ambiguity concerning the importance and supremacy of the Official Languages Act which, coupled with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, happens to be the legal foundations of that linguistic equality. In short, the purpose of this Bill is to assert the political will of this Parliament with respect to the supremacy of the Official Languages Act.
Bill C-203, about which this Parliament is called upon to make a decision, is aimed at asserting the primacy of Official
Languages Act Section 2 over any other legislative and regulatory provision of the Parliament and the Government of Canada. Secondarily, it also stipulates that banks and railway companies shall publish, in Canada's both official languages, certain notices and other documents intended for the public. The Acts to be amended now prescribe that only in the Province of Quebec shall they publish certain notices and documents in French and English.
Section 2 of the Official Languages Act passed in 1969 says the following:
The English and French languages are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada, and possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada.
It was therefore 15 years ago that this Parliament decided to legislate to entrench the principle of linguistic equality in the Canadian Federation. This was an important decision, a symbol of the progress made at the time. However, legally, the Official Languages Act does not necessarily have supremacy over other pieces of legislation passed by this Parliament. However, in our legal system, depending on how the general principles of interpretation of our laws are applied, Section 2 of the Official Languages Act might not have precedence over another legislative provision where there is a conflict. The courts have even recognized that a simple regulation may occasionally, in case of conflict, have supremacy over Section 2 of the Official Languages Act.
Mr. Speaker, this is basically the situation which Bill C-203 wants to change. From now on, if the Bill is passed, in case of a conflict between Section 2 of the Official Languages Act and another federal Act or Regulation, Section 2 would have precedence. I invite the Hon. Members to read the proceedings of the Committee on Official Languages, which was first a Special Joint Committee and is now a Standing Committee, on this issue to learn about the full impact of this Bill.
This Parliament would clearly establish that, as a first step, the courts would attempt to see whether it is possible to interpret federal Acts and Regulations in such a way that they would not cancel, restrict or violate the rule stated in Section 2. If this proves impossible, they would have to give precedence to Section 2, and any other legislative or regulatory provision in conflict with it could be declared nul and void. However, Bill C-203 leaves Parliament free to go against Section 2 of the Official Languages Act by an express statement to this purpose. Thus by giving Parliament the right to go against Section 2 Parliament would be fully empowered to make the political decisions it deems appropriate to ensure linguistic equality in federal institutions. Thus, while some progress will be made as far as linguistic equality is concerned, exceptions to this principle will still be possible.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, I invite my colleagues in this House to examine the submissions made to the Committee in this regard. For instance, there was the submission made by Professor Gerald Beaudoin, who told us clearly and precisely that, in fact, the purpose of such a clause was to give to the
December 17, 1984

Official Languages Act supremacy over any other piece of legislation so that it would have the status of a linguistic charter.
If the Official Languages Act contains a provision which allows Parliament to make exceptions, this also provides some flexibility and thus establishes a linguistic charter, which is essential in my opinion.
The principle contained in Bill C-203 has already been approved by the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Official Languages. Hon. Members will recall that this Committee was asked to examine Bill C-214 introduced during the previous Parliament, whose purpose was the same as that of the bill now before us. It made a recommendation to that effect, even though the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms enshrines this in almost similar terms, in its Section 16 that is well known to us all. It is the same wording, the same principle. The Official Languages act, as pointed out by a witness in Committee, and I quote:
-can cover fields that are not directly provided for in Section 16 of the Charter of Rights.
To illustrate, Mr. Speaker, let me add that the coming into force in 1982 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has not done away with the relevancy of the Canadian Bill of Rights. On the contrary, it will be remembered that the Canadian Bill of Rights Act was enacted in 1960 and that we also passed in 1977 the Canadian Human Rights Act.
That has not changed anything, those Acts are still in the books and they do not conflict with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Official Languages Act, especially Section 2, therefore remains a necessary element to the promotion of linguistic equality in federal institutions in this country. Bill C-203 proposes to give precedence to that principle, while providing Parliament with a notwithstanding clause. Briefly, such is the extent of the measure submitted to this House.
In a non-partisan spirit, Mr. Speaker, let us now look at the political aspect.
In the Throne Speech, the Government stated on November 5, 1984, and I quote:
My government is committed to ensuring that the equality of the two official languages-so vital to our national character and identity-is respected in fact as it is in law. My Ministers acknowledge the need for ongoing improvements and for vigilance in this indispensable area of our national life.
This is a goal I endorse wholeheartedly, Mr. Speaker, but we are forced to conclude that the Government is not very specific with respect to its legislative intentions. It is my view that if this Parliament were to give all the attention needed to Bill C-203 1 am introducing today, a major step would be made in respect of the linguistic reform started in 1969.
Since 1969, the linguistic reform has made undeniable progress. Within the three political parties in this House, there is at the official level at least a wide consensus on the principle of linguistic equality and its implementation. As evidence you have the two resolutions passed by this House during the previous Parliament at the time of the linguistic crisis in
Official Languages Act
Manitoba and the three-party consensus which marked the proceedings in the Special Joint Committee on Official Languages, to which 1 referred earlier and of which 1 was a co-chairman.
You will also remember, Mr. Speaker, the wide consensus which prevailed when the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was adopted, which as we know included important linguistic provisions. The fact remains, however, that the Official Languages Act is somewhat outdated. In many respects, it does not reflect the progress made in the linguistic reform process it had launched and which, in the view of some people, it is not hindering. I am thinking especially of the whole question of language in the work place within the Public Service of Canada. Linguistic equality having been enshrined at the highest level in the Constitutional Act of 1982, consistency now requires that we do more, that we give the Official Languages Act the status it deserves. In so doing, this Parliament will clearly indicate to the Canadian people its determination to actualize the principle of linguistic equality.
Language tensions are still a political fact of life in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Recent events in New Brunswick and Manitoba show that the road to linguistic equality is not an easy one. French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians need reassurance from the federal legislators that, despite the pitfalls, there is unswerving determination at the national level to attain linguistic equality. This is the least we can do, Mr. Speaker, and I conclude my remarks on Bill C-203 by expressing the hope that I will get the support of Hon. Members, in order that the motion on this legislation may carry today.
In past years, Mr. Speaker, one or our colleagues would suggest that the Bill be deferred to a committee for consideration. I think that such an issue could be covered in a resolution by a member of this House. I would greatly appreciate it if this very important and extremely relevant question could be thoroughly dealt with by the joint Committees on Official Languages Policy and Programs chaired by a government member. I think that the committee should meet and thoroughly examine the proposal so that one day true linguistic equality will be achieved in this country.
